stem: The chapter 'Framing the Constitution' deals with the making of the Indian Constitution by the __________.
options: Constituent Assembly
British Parliament
Indian National Congress alone
Supreme Court
solution: The chapter deals with the making of the Indian Constitution by the Constituent Assembly — the body of elected representatives entrusted with framing the Constitution of independent India. It examines the debates, ideals, compromises, and key figures involved in drafting the document that would govern the new nation. So the Constitution was framed by the Constituent Assembly. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The Constituent Assembly that framed the Indian Constitution held its sessions mainly between __________.
options: December 1946 and 1949 (the Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950)
solution: The Constituent Assembly first met in December 1946 and carried on its work through the momentous years of independence and Partition. It completed the Constitution, which was ADOPTED on 26 November 1949 (now celebrated as Constitution Day) and CAME INTO FORCE on 26 January 1950 (Republic Day). The Assembly deliberated for nearly three years. So its main period of work was December 1946 to 1949. This is a prelims-critical set of dates.

stem: The Constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950. This date was chosen because it was already significant as __________.
options: 'Independence Day'/Purna Swaraj Day, first observed on 26 January 1930 (the anniversary of the Congress's 1929–30 complete-independence pledge)
Gandhi's birthday
The day the British left India
The date of the Jallianwala Bagh massacre
solution: The Constitution was brought into force on 26 January 1950 to honour the significance this date already held: on 26 January 1930, the Indian National Congress (following its Purna Swaraj resolution at the Lahore session of December 1929) had first observed 'INDEPENDENCE DAY' / Purna Swaraj Day, pledging complete independence. Choosing 26 January 1950 as the day the Republic was inaugurated thus linked the new Constitution to that historic pledge. So the date honoured the 1930 'Independence Day' observance. This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: The Chairman of the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly, often called the 'chief architect' of the Indian Constitution, was __________.
options: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
Jawaharlal Nehru
Rajendra Prasad
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
solution: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was the Chairman of the DRAFTING COMMITTEE of the Constituent Assembly and is widely regarded as the 'chief architect' (principal draftsman) of the Indian Constitution. A brilliant jurist and champion of the depressed classes, he played the leading role in drafting and steering the Constitution through the Assembly. (He also served as independent India's first Law Minister.) So the Chairman of the Drafting Committee was Dr. B.R. Ambedkar. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: The President (Chairman) of the Constituent Assembly, who presided over its sessions and later became India's first President, was __________.
options: Dr. Rajendra Prasad
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar
C. Rajagopalachari
Jawaharlal Nehru
solution: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the President (Chairman) of the Constituent Assembly, presiding over its deliberations. He later became the FIRST PRESIDENT of the Republic of India (1950). (Note the distinction: Rajendra Prasad presided over the Assembly, while Dr. B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.) So the President of the Constituent Assembly was Dr. Rajendra Prasad. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: Jawaharlal Nehru moved the famous __________ in the Constituent Assembly, which laid down the ideals and objectives that were to guide the framing of the Constitution.
options: Objectives Resolution
Rowlatt Resolution
Non-Cooperation Resolution
Partition Resolution
solution: Jawaharlal Nehru moved the famous 'OBJECTIVES RESOLUTION' in the Constituent Assembly (in December 1946). It laid down the fundamental IDEALS and OBJECTIVES that were to guide the framing of the Constitution — proclaiming India as an independent, sovereign republic, and guaranteeing to all its people justice, equality, and freedom (liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith, and worship), and safeguards for minorities and the depressed/backward classes. Its ideals were later reflected in the Preamble of the Constitution. So Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The Constituent Assembly did its detailed work largely through __________.
options: Numerous committees and sub-committees (whose reports were debated in the full Assembly), with expert advice and extensive discussion
A single day of voting with no discussion
Decisions taken solely by the British Viceroy
A public referendum on every article
solution: The Constituent Assembly accomplished its enormous task largely through NUMEROUS COMMITTEES and sub-committees (such as those on fundamental rights, minorities, union powers, and the drafting committee), each of which studied particular questions and prepared reports and drafts. These were then DEBATED clause by clause in the full Assembly, informed by EXPERT ADVICE (e.g., the constitutional adviser B.N. Rau) and EXTENSIVE, careful DISCUSSION. This deliberative, committee-based process, spread over nearly three years, allowed thorough consideration of the many complex issues. So the Assembly worked through committees and detailed debate. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A central and hotly debated question in the Constituent Assembly was the relationship between the CENTRE and the STATES (provinces), i.e., the question of __________.
options: Federalism — how to divide powers between a strong central government and the states/provinces
Whether to have any government at all
The colour of the national flag
Whether to keep the British monarch
solution: One of the central and most hotly debated questions in the Constituent Assembly was the CENTRE–STATE relationship — the question of FEDERALISM, i.e., how to divide powers and resources between a CENTRAL (Union) government and the STATES/provinces. In the context of Partition and the fears of fragmentation, many members (and Ambedkar) favoured a relatively STRONG CENTRE to ensure national unity, stability, and coordinated development, while others argued for greater powers and autonomy for the states/provinces. The Constitution ultimately established a federal system with a strong centralising tilt. So the debate was over federalism/centre–state powers. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Given the trauma of Partition and the need to hold a diverse country together, many members (including Ambedkar) argued for __________.
options: A strong central government (a powerful Centre) to preserve national unity and prevent fragmentation
The abolition of the central government
Complete independence for every village
Handing power back to the princes
solution: In the shadow of the trauma of PARTITION and the fears of further FRAGMENTATION and disorder in a vast and DIVERSE country, many members of the Constituent Assembly — including Dr. Ambedkar — argued strongly for a STRONG CENTRAL government (a powerful Centre). They believed a strong Centre was necessary to PRESERVE national UNITY and integrity, to maintain order and stability, and to plan and coordinate the country's economic and social development. This concern shaped the Constitution's federal design, which gave significant powers to the Union. So many favoured a strong Centre to preserve unity. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Another major issue was the position of the many different LANGUAGES of India. The debate over which language should be the 'national'/official language was especially contentious regarding __________.
options: Hindi (and whether/how it should be the official language, versus the concerns of non-Hindi-speaking regions)
Latin
Sanskrit as the sole spoken language
English becoming the only language forever
solution: The LANGUAGE question was one of the most contentious in the Constituent Assembly. There was intense debate over whether HINDI should be made the 'national' or official language of India. Advocates of Hindi pushed for its adoption as the national language, while members from NON-HINDI-speaking regions (especially the south and east) were deeply concerned that this would disadvantage their languages and peoples. The eventual COMPROMISE (the 'Munshi–Ayyangar formula') made HINDI (in Devanagari script) the OFFICIAL language of the Union, while allowing the continued use of ENGLISH for official purposes (initially for fifteen years, and thereafter as provided), and recognising many regional languages. So the contentious language issue centred on Hindi. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The resolution of the language dispute involved a compromise whereby __________.
options: Hindi was made the official language of the Union, but English would continue to be used for official purposes for a period, and many regional languages were recognised
Only Hindi would ever be used, immediately
English was banned outright
Every citizen had to learn all Indian languages
solution: The language dispute was resolved through a CAREFUL COMPROMISE (associated with the 'Munshi–Ayyangar formula'). Under it: HINDI (in the Devanagari script) was made the OFFICIAL LANGUAGE of the Union; but the use of ENGLISH for official purposes was to CONTINUE for a period (initially fifteen years, and could be extended), to reassure non-Hindi speakers and ensure a gradual transition; and many regional languages were recognised (listed in the Eighth Schedule). Notably, Hindi was made the 'official' language rather than the 'national' language, in deference to India's linguistic diversity. So the compromise made Hindi the official language while retaining English for a period and recognising regional languages. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The question of the rights and safeguards of the DEPRESSED CLASSES (Scheduled Castes) and minorities was addressed. A key measure adopted for the depressed classes and tribes was __________.
options: The abolition of untouchability and the provision of reservations (reserved seats in legislatures and other safeguards) for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
Their exclusion from citizenship
Separate electorates permanently
No measures at all
solution: The Constituent Assembly addressed the rights and safeguards of the DEPRESSED CLASSES (Scheduled Castes) and tribes. Key measures adopted included: the ABOLITION of UNTOUCHABILITY (made a fundamental provision — Article 17); and the provision of RESERVATIONS — reserved SEATS in the legislatures (Lok Sabha and state assemblies) for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and other safeguards to promote their upliftment and representation. (Separate electorates, however, were NOT adopted; the earlier demand for them gave way to reserved seats within joint electorates, in line with the spirit of the Poona Pact.) So the measures included abolishing untouchability and providing reservations. So option 1 is correct.

stem: During the debates, some members from the depressed classes argued that mere legal abolition of untouchability was not enough; the real problem was __________.
options: The deep-rooted social attitudes and structures of the caste system, which needed to be changed for true equality and dignity
The lack of enough laws in general
Too much education
The absence of a strong Centre
solution: During the debates, some members from the depressed classes argued powerfully that merely ABOLISHING untouchability by LAW would NOT be enough. The DEEPER problem, they contended, lay in the entrenched SOCIAL ATTITUDES, prejudices, and STRUCTURES of the CASTE SYSTEM itself — the discrimination, exclusion, and denial of dignity woven into society. True EQUALITY and DIGNITY for the oppressed, they insisted, required not just legal provisions but a fundamental TRANSFORMATION of social attitudes and relations, and positive measures (like reservations and access to public spaces, education, and temples) to overcome centuries of oppression. So the real problem identified was the deep-rooted social structure of caste. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Constituent Assembly's members represented a wide range of views and interests, yet they generally worked to __________.
options: Reach consensus and accommodate diverse views through debate and compromise, in the larger interest of the nation
Impose one group's will by force with no discussion
Copy the British system without any change
Avoid all disagreement by not debating
solution: The members of the Constituent Assembly came from varied backgrounds and held a WIDE RANGE of views and interests (on federalism, language, rights, religion, economic policy, and the concerns of different communities, regions, and classes). Yet the striking feature of the Assembly was that its members generally worked to REACH CONSENSUS and to ACCOMMODATE these diverse views through reasoned DEBATE, persuasion, and COMPROMISE — subordinating narrower interests to the LARGER INTEREST of the NATION. Difficult issues were resolved not by force but by discussion and mutual give-and-take. This spirit of accommodation and consensus-building is a celebrated aspect of the Constitution-making process. So the members worked to reach consensus through debate and compromise. So option 1 is correct.

stem: A rich and valuable source that historians use to study the making of the Constitution is __________.
options: The Constituent Assembly Debates (the verbatim record of the discussions in the Assembly)
Mughal court chronicles
The Rig Veda
Colonial revenue records
solution: A rich and invaluable source for studying the making of the Constitution is the CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY DEBATES — the VERBATIM RECORD (the official transcripts) of the discussions, speeches, arguments, and deliberations that took place in the Assembly. These debates preserve the views, reasoning, hopes, fears, and disagreements of the members on every major issue, allowing historians to understand HOW and WHY the Constitution took the shape it did. The chapter draws heavily on these debates. So the key source is the Constituent Assembly Debates. This is a prelims-relevant methodological point.

stem: The core values enshrined in the Constitution (as expressed in its Preamble) include __________.
options: Justice, Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity (and India as a sovereign, democratic republic)
Monarchy and aristocracy
Colonial rule and racial hierarchy
The supremacy of one religion
solution: The core VALUES enshrined in the Constitution, as expressed in its PREAMBLE, include: JUSTICE (social, economic, and political), LIBERTY (of thought, expression, belief, faith, and worship), EQUALITY (of status and opportunity), and FRATERNITY (assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity of the nation) — with India declared a SOVEREIGN, DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC (later amended to also include 'Socialist, Secular'). These ideals (drawn from the freedom struggle and the Objectives Resolution) form the philosophical foundation of the Constitution. So the core values include justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Constitution guaranteed a set of FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS to citizens. These were meant to __________.
options: Protect the basic freedoms and equality of individuals and safeguard citizens (including minorities and the oppressed) against arbitrary state action and discrimination
Give unlimited power to the government
Apply only to the rich
Restrict citizens' freedoms
solution: The Constitution guaranteed a set of FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS to citizens (such as the right to equality, freedom of speech and expression, freedom of religion, cultural and educational rights, and the right to constitutional remedies). These rights were meant to PROTECT the basic FREEDOMS and EQUALITY of individuals, and to SAFEGUARD citizens — including MINORITIES and the OPPRESSED/depressed classes — against arbitrary or discriminatory action by the STATE (and against social discrimination, e.g., the abolition of untouchability). They embody the liberal-democratic commitment to individual liberty and dignity. So the fundamental rights protect basic freedoms and equality and safeguard against arbitrary state action. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following pairs of a leader with his role in the Constituent Assembly is CORRECT?
options: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar — Chairman of the Drafting Committee; Dr. Rajendra Prasad — President of the Assembly; Jawaharlal Nehru — mover of the Objectives Resolution
Ambedkar — President of the Assembly; Nehru — Chairman of the Drafting Committee
Rajendra Prasad — Chairman of the Drafting Committee; Ambedkar — mover of the Objectives Resolution
Patel — President of the Assembly; Nehru — Chairman of the Drafting Committee
solution: The correct roles are: Dr. B.R. AMBEDKAR — Chairman of the DRAFTING COMMITTEE (chief architect of the Constitution); Dr. Rajendra PRASAD — PRESIDENT (Chairman) of the Constituent Assembly (who presided over it, and later became first President of India); and Jawaharlal NEHRU — who moved the OBJECTIVES RESOLUTION (and was also involved in key committees). Other notable figures included Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel (who chaired important committees, e.g., on fundamental rights and minorities) and the constitutional adviser B.N. Rau. So option 1 gives the correct pairings. This is prelims-relevant.

stem: The debates over religion and the state led the framers to adopt the principle of __________ for India.
options: Secularism (the state would not favour or establish any one religion; equal respect/treatment for all religions)
A single official state religion
The banning of all religion
Rule by religious priests
solution: The debates over the relationship between RELIGION and the STATE — sharpened by the communal violence of Partition and the presence of many religious communities — led the framers to adopt the principle of SECULARISM for India. The Indian state would NOT establish or favour any one religion; it would treat ALL religions with EQUAL respect (and non-interference/even-handedness), and guarantee FREEDOM of religion to all citizens, while ensuring that citizenship and rights did not depend on religion. (This secular character was implicit in the Constitution from the start and the word 'secular' was later explicitly added to the Preamble.) So the framers adopted secularism. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The framing of the Constitution took place amid the backdrop of __________, which deeply influenced the debates (e.g., on unity, minorities, and a strong Centre).
options: The Partition of India and the accompanying communal violence and refugee crisis
A period of total peace and prosperity
A foreign invasion of India
The Industrial Revolution
solution: The Constitution was framed amid the traumatic backdrop of the PARTITION of India (1947) and the accompanying horrific COMMUNAL VIOLENCE and massive REFUGEE crisis. This grim context deeply INFLUENCED the debates in the Constituent Assembly: it heightened concerns about national UNITY and integrity (strengthening the case for a strong Centre), about the protection and rights of MINORITIES (and the rejection of separate electorates in favour of a secular, common citizenship), and about building a stable, inclusive, and just order out of the wreckage. So the framing occurred against the backdrop of Partition and communal violence. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Assertion (A): The framers of the Constitution favoured a strong central government. Reason (R): The Partition and the danger of national disintegration made national unity and stability an overriding concern. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the framers (including Ambedkar) largely favoured a STRONG CENTRAL government. And the reason is (R) that the trauma of PARTITION and the real danger of national DISINTEGRATION/fragmentation made preserving national UNITY, integrity, and STABILITY an overriding concern. A strong Centre was seen as essential to hold the diverse, newly independent, and recently divided country together, maintain order, and coordinate development. So this overriding concern for unity in the wake of Partition directly explains the preference for a strong Centre (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): The Constituent Assembly Debates are a valuable historical source. Reason (R): They record the actual arguments, ideals, disagreements, and compromises of the members, revealing how and why the Constitution was shaped as it was. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the Constituent Assembly Debates are a valuable historical source. And the reason is (R) that they RECORD the actual ARGUMENTS, IDEALS, DISAGREEMENTS, and COMPROMISES of the members on every major issue — thereby REVEALING how and why the Constitution came to be shaped as it was (the reasoning behind its provisions, the concerns that were weighed, and the negotiations that resolved them). This is precisely what makes the debates so valuable to historians (A). So R correctly explains A. This underscores the chapter's methodological emphasis on the debates as a source.

stem: The making of the Indian Constitution is often admired because __________.
options: Despite immense challenges and deep differences, it produced a democratic, inclusive framework through debate and consensus — a lengthy, detailed constitution reflecting the ideals of the freedom struggle and the aspirations of a diverse people
It was written in a single day without any thought
It simply copied another country's constitution unchanged
It excluded most Indians from rights
solution: The making of the Indian Constitution is widely admired because, DESPITE immense CHALLENGES (Partition, communal violence, poverty, and enormous diversity) and DEEP DIFFERENCES among the members, the Constituent Assembly succeeded — through sustained DEBATE, accommodation, and CONSENSUS-building — in producing a DEMOCRATIC, INCLUSIVE constitutional framework. The result was a lengthy, detailed, and carefully considered Constitution that enshrined the IDEALS of the freedom struggle (democracy, justice, liberty, equality, fraternity, secularism, and safeguards for the weak) and sought to meet the ASPIRATIONS of a vast and diverse people (while drawing selectively and thoughtfully on the experience of other constitutions and India's own history). So it is admired for building a democratic, inclusive framework through consensus amid great challenges. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Constitution was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on __________.
options: 26 November 1949
15 August 1947
26 January 1930
2 October 1948
solution: The Indian Constitution was ADOPTED by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949 (this day is now observed as 'Constitution Day' / Samvidhan Divas). It then CAME INTO FORCE on 26 January 1950 (Republic Day). So the Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949. This is a prelims-relevant date to distinguish from the date it came into effect.

stem: The constitutional adviser to the Constituent Assembly, who prepared an initial draft and provided expert guidance, was __________.
options: B.N. Rau (Sir Benegal Narsing Rau)
B.R. Ambedkar
Rajendra Prasad
Sardar Patel
solution: B.N. Rau (Sir Benegal Narsing Rau) was the Constitutional Adviser to the Constituent Assembly. A distinguished jurist, he prepared an initial DRAFT of the Constitution and provided expert legal and constitutional GUIDANCE to the Assembly and its committees (studying constitutions of other countries and framing preliminary drafts), which the Drafting Committee (under Ambedkar) then worked upon. So the constitutional adviser was B.N. Rau. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The members of the Constituent Assembly were elected __________.
options: Indirectly, mainly by the members of the provincial legislative assemblies (which had themselves been elected on a limited franchise)
By direct universal adult vote of all Indians
By the British Parliament
By the princely rulers alone
solution: The members of the Constituent Assembly were elected INDIRECTLY — chiefly by the members of the PROVINCIAL Legislative Assemblies (which had themselves been elected earlier on a LIMITED/restricted franchise, not full universal suffrage), with additional members nominated by the princely states. Thus the Assembly was not directly elected by all adult Indians. Despite this indirect and limited-franchise origin, the Assembly is generally seen as broadly representative of India's major communities, regions, and interests, and it framed a Constitution granting UNIVERSAL ADULT FRANCHISE to the people. So the members were elected indirectly by provincial assemblies. This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: A landmark democratic decision of the framers was to grant the right to vote to __________.
options: All adult citizens (universal adult franchise/suffrage), regardless of caste, class, religion, education, property, or gender
Only property-owning men
Only the educated elite
Only men above 30
solution: A landmark and bold democratic decision of the framers was to grant UNIVERSAL ADULT FRANCHISE (suffrage) — the right to VOTE to ALL adult citizens, regardless of CASTE, CLASS, RELIGION, EDUCATION, PROPERTY, or GENDER. This was a remarkable and courageous step, especially for a poor country with mass illiteracy and deep social divisions, at a time when many older democracies had only gradually extended the franchise. It expressed a profound faith in democracy and the equality and political dignity of every citizen. So the framers granted universal adult franchise. This is a prelims-critical fact.

stem: Granting universal adult franchise was considered remarkable/courageous because __________.
options: India was a vast, poor country with widespread illiteracy and deep social inequalities, yet the framers trusted ordinary people with the vote (unlike many countries that had extended the franchise only gradually)
Very few people lived in India
Everyone was already highly educated
It was demanded by the British
solution: Granting universal adult franchise at the very outset was considered remarkable and COURAGEOUS because India was an ENORMOUS, POOR country with WIDESPREAD ILLITERACY and DEEP SOCIAL INEQUALITIES (of caste, class, and gender). Many contemporaries doubted whether such a population could exercise the vote responsibly, and in most other countries the franchise had been extended only GRADUALLY (over decades, first to propertied men, then more widely). Yet the framers of the Indian Constitution boldly reposed their FAITH in ordinary people and in democracy, giving every adult an equal vote immediately. So it was remarkable given India's poverty, illiteracy, and inequalities, and the framers' trust in the people. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Alongside Fundamental Rights, the Constitution also included non-justiciable guidelines for the state to promote social and economic welfare, called the __________.
options: Directive Principles of State Policy
Preamble
Fundamental Duties
Seventh Schedule
solution: Alongside the (justiciable) Fundamental Rights, the Constitution included the DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES OF STATE POLICY — a set of GUIDELINES/directives (non-justiciable, i.e., not enforceable in courts) instructing the STATE to promote the social and economic WELFARE of the people and to work toward a just society (e.g., securing adequate livelihood, reducing inequalities, providing for education, public health, and the welfare of workers and the weaker sections). They express the ideal of a welfare state and set social/economic goals for governance. So these guidelines are the Directive Principles of State Policy. This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: Some members in the Assembly wanted the Constitution to reflect Gandhian ideals, arguing for greater emphasis on __________.
options: Village panchayats / village self-government and decentralisation (making the village the basic unit)
Heavy industrialisation only
A powerful monarchy
Abolishing all local government
solution: Some members of the Constituent Assembly, inspired by GANDHIAN ideals, argued that the Constitution should give greater emphasis to the VILLAGE — advocating VILLAGE PANCHAYATS and village self-government, and DECENTRALISATION of power, with the village as the basic unit of Indian democracy and administration (in keeping with Gandhi's vision of village-centred 'gram swaraj'). Others (like Ambedkar) were sceptical, viewing villages as sites of caste oppression and backwardness and preferring a more centralised, individual-rights-based framework. In the end, the Constitution adopted a strong Centre and individual citizenship, but the ideal of panchayats found expression in the Directive Principles (and was strengthened much later by the 73rd Amendment). So the Gandhian members emphasised village panchayats/decentralisation. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The Constitution adopted for independent India was notably __________ compared with those of many other countries.
options: Very lengthy and detailed (one of the longest written constitutions in the world)
Extremely short with only a few lines
Entirely unwritten
Written only in English poetry
solution: The Indian Constitution is notably VERY LENGTHY and DETAILED — it is one of the LONGEST written constitutions in the world. Its great length reflects the framers' attempt to address the complexities and diversity of India, to spell out matters in detail (leaving little ambiguous), to incorporate provisions covering the Union and the states, fundamental rights and directive principles, and safeguards for many groups, and to draw on the experience of many other constitutions and India's own administrative history. So the Indian Constitution is very lengthy and detailed. This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: The framers studied and borrowed selectively from the constitutions and experiences of other countries. This shows that they __________.
options: Learned from global experience but adapted borrowed features to Indian conditions and needs (rather than blindly copying)
Copied one foreign constitution word for word
Rejected all outside ideas entirely
Had no knowledge of other countries
solution: In framing the Constitution, the members STUDIED and BORROWED SELECTIVELY from the constitutions and experiences of many other countries (e.g., features of parliamentary government, fundamental rights, federalism, directive principles, and judicial review drawn from British, American, Irish, Canadian, and other models). But they did NOT blindly copy any single foreign constitution; rather, they LEARNED from global experience and ADAPTED the borrowed features to India's own CONDITIONS, needs, and realities (also drawing on India's own administrative and political experience, e.g., the Government of India Act 1935). So the framers learned from global experience while adapting it to India. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The debate on whether to include the word/ideal reflecting India's economic direction (and the role of the state in the economy) reflected differing visions of __________.
options: Social and economic justice — how far the state should act to reduce inequality and promote the welfare of the poor (reflected especially in the Directive Principles)
The national anthem
Foreign policy alone
The design of currency notes
solution: Debates touching on India's economic direction and the role of the state reflected differing visions of SOCIAL and ECONOMIC JUSTICE — in particular, HOW FAR the STATE should actively intervene to REDUCE inequalities (of wealth, land, and opportunity) and to promote the WELFARE and upliftment of the poor and weaker sections. Some pressed for stronger commitments to economic equality and social transformation; the resulting balance was expressed especially through the DIRECTIVE PRINCIPLES of State Policy (which set goals like reducing inequality and securing welfare) alongside the guarantee of individual rights. So the debate reflected differing visions of social and economic justice. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The concerns of the tribal peoples (Adivasis) were also raised in the Assembly, notably by members like Jaipal Singh, who argued for __________.
options: Safeguards and provisions to protect tribal peoples' interests, land, and dignity, and to integrate them into the nation while respecting their distinct identity
The exclusion of tribals from India
Denying tribals any rights
Abolishing all tribal communities
solution: The concerns of the TRIBAL peoples (Adivasis) were raised in the Constituent Assembly, notably by members such as Jaipal Singh (himself a distinguished Adivasi leader). He and others argued for SAFEGUARDS and special PROVISIONS to protect the tribal peoples' interests, their LAND and resources, and their DIGNITY — to guard against exploitation by outsiders and to promote their upliftment — while INTEGRATING them into the national mainstream in a way that RESPECTED their distinct IDENTITY and way of life. The Constitution accordingly provided reservations for Scheduled Tribes and special provisions for tribal areas (e.g., the Fifth and Sixth Schedules). So the tribal members sought safeguards and provisions for tribal interests and dignity. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The intense debates in the Constituent Assembly, and the compromises reached, demonstrate that the Constitution was __________.
options: The product of reasoned deliberation, negotiation, and accommodation among people with genuinely different views and interests — not a document handed down by any single authority
Dictated by one person alone
Decided by lottery
Written without any disagreement
solution: The intense DEBATES and the many COMPROMISES reached in the Constituent Assembly demonstrate that the Constitution was the PRODUCT of REASONED DELIBERATION, NEGOTIATION, and ACCOMMODATION among people who held genuinely DIFFERENT views and represented different interests, communities, regions, and ideologies. Difficult questions (federalism, language, minority rights, the role of the state) were thrashed out through argument and mutual give-and-take, and resolved by consensus and compromise in the national interest. Thus the Constitution was NOT simply handed down by any single authority or individual; it emerged from a collective, democratic process of deliberation. So option 1 is correct. This is an important point about the nature of the Constitution.

stem: By studying the Constituent Assembly Debates, historians can appreciate __________.
options: The hopes, fears, ideals, and reasoning of the framers, and the diversity of views that were reconciled — giving insight into the meaning and spirit behind the Constitution's provisions
Only the price of paper in 1949
The weather during the sessions
Nothing of importance
solution: By studying the CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY DEBATES, historians can appreciate the HOPES, FEARS, IDEALS, and REASONING of the framers — the arguments they advanced, the concerns they weighed, and the DIVERSITY of views (across region, community, class, and ideology) that had to be RECONCILED. This gives valuable insight into the MEANING and SPIRIT behind the Constitution's provisions (why particular choices were made, and what the framers intended), enriching our understanding of the document beyond its bare text. So the debates reveal the framers' hopes, ideals, and reasoning. So option 1 is correct. This underscores why the debates are such an important source.

stem: Assertion (A): The framers granted universal adult franchise from the very beginning. Reason (R): They believed in the principle of political equality and democracy, trusting all citizens — regardless of status — with an equal share in choosing their government. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the framers granted UNIVERSAL ADULT FRANCHISE from the very beginning of the Republic. And the reason is (R) that they believed deeply in the principle of POLITICAL EQUALITY and DEMOCRACY — trusting ALL citizens, regardless of caste, class, gender, wealth, or education, with an EQUAL share in choosing their government. This faith in the equal political worth and dignity of every citizen directly explains their decision to extend the vote to all adults at once (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: Assertion (A): The Constitution abolished untouchability. Reason (R): The framers were committed to social justice and the equal dignity of all citizens, and sought to end centuries of caste-based oppression. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the Constitution ABOLISHED untouchability (Article 17) and forbade its practice in any form. And the reason is (R) that the framers were committed to SOCIAL JUSTICE and to the EQUAL DIGNITY of all citizens, and were determined to END the centuries of caste-based OPPRESSION and degradation suffered by the depressed classes. This commitment to equality and dignity, and the resolve to undo caste injustice, directly explain the abolition of untouchability (A). So R correctly explains A.

stem: The Constitution declared India to be a __________ (the form of the state as expressed in the Preamble and Objectives Resolution).
options: Sovereign democratic republic
British dominion under the monarch
Theocratic state
Military dictatorship
solution: The Constitution (following the ideals of the Objectives Resolution and as expressed in the PREAMBLE) declared India to be a SOVEREIGN DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC — 'sovereign' (fully independent, subject to no external authority), 'democratic' (government by the people, based on universal adult franchise), and a 'republic' (with an elected head of state, not a hereditary monarch). (The words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added to the Preamble later, by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.) So the Constitution declared India a sovereign democratic republic. This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: The chapter 'Framing the Constitution' is the concluding chapter of the Class 12 History syllabus, and it marks __________.
options: The transition from the colonial era to independent, democratic India — 'the beginning of a new era'
The start of the Mughal Empire
The Harappan civilisation
The medieval bhakti movement
solution: The chapter 'Framing the Constitution' (subtitled 'The Beginning of a New Era') is the concluding chapter of the Class 12 History course. It marks the momentous TRANSITION from the COLONIAL era (and the long freedom struggle) to INDEPENDENT, democratic, republican India — the founding of a new political order based on the Constitution. It thus fittingly closes the study of Indian history at the threshold of the modern republic — 'the beginning of a new era'. So the chapter marks the transition to independent, democratic India. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The rejection of SEPARATE ELECTORATES (which had existed under British rule) by the Constituent Assembly reflected the framers' commitment to __________.
options: A common, shared citizenship and national unity — avoiding the institutional division of the electorate along religious lines (seen as having contributed to Partition)
Permanent religious division
The supremacy of one community
Denying anyone the vote
solution: Under British rule, SEPARATE ELECTORATES (where members of a particular religious community voted separately for their own representatives) had existed, and were widely seen as having deepened communal divisions and contributed to PARTITION. The Constituent Assembly, after debate, REJECTED separate electorates for the future. This reflected the framers' commitment to a COMMON, SHARED CITIZENSHIP and NATIONAL UNITY — a single, joint electorate in which all citizens voted together as Indians, rather than being institutionally divided along religious lines. (Safeguards for minorities and the depressed classes were instead provided through other means, like reserved seats within joint electorates.) So rejecting separate electorates reflected a commitment to common citizenship and unity. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The framers provided for an INDEPENDENT judiciary and mechanisms like the right to constitutional remedies because they wanted __________.
options: To protect citizens' fundamental rights and uphold the Constitution, with courts able to check violations by the state
The government to have unlimited unchecked power
To abolish all courts
Judges to be appointed by a foreign power
solution: The framers provided for an INDEPENDENT JUDICIARY and for mechanisms such as the RIGHT to CONSTITUTIONAL REMEDIES (which Ambedkar called the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution — the right to move the courts to enforce fundamental rights) because they wanted to PROTECT citizens' FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS and to UPHOLD the Constitution. An independent judiciary empowered to review and CHECK violations by the state ensures that rights are not merely paper guarantees but can be enforced, and that governmental power remains within constitutional limits (the rule of law). So these provisions were meant to protect rights and check state power. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Which of the following correctly matches the date with the event?
options: Dec 1946 — Constituent Assembly first meets/Objectives Resolution; 26 Nov 1949 — Constitution adopted; 26 Jan 1950 — Constitution comes into force (Republic Day)
26 Jan 1950 — Constituent Assembly first meets; 1946 — Constitution comes into force
15 Aug 1947 — Constitution adopted; 1949 — Assembly first meets
26 Nov 1949 — Republic Day; 26 Jan 1950 — Constitution adopted
solution: The correct matching is: DECEMBER 1946 — the Constituent Assembly first MEETS (and Nehru soon moves the Objectives Resolution); 26 NOVEMBER 1949 — the Constitution is ADOPTED by the Assembly (Constitution Day); and 26 JANUARY 1950 — the Constitution COMES INTO FORCE, and India becomes a Republic (Republic Day). Knowing these dates precisely — and distinguishing the date of adoption (26 Nov 1949) from the date of coming into force (26 Jan 1950) — is prelims-critical. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The framers' decision to make India a SECULAR state (treating all religions equally) was strongly influenced by __________.
options: The experience of communal conflict and Partition, and the presence of many religious communities within India — making equal treatment of all faiths essential to unity and justice
A desire to establish one national religion
The wish to ban religion
Pressure from a foreign country
solution: The framers' commitment to making India a SECULAR state — one that treats ALL religions EQUALLY, does not establish or favour any one religion, and guarantees freedom of religion to all — was strongly influenced by the recent experience of COMMUNAL CONFLICT and the trauma of PARTITION, and by the reality that India was home to MANY religious COMMUNITIES (Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs, Christians, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis, and others). In such a diverse society, and after the horrors of communal violence, EQUAL treatment of all faiths and a state that stood above religious partisanship were seen as ESSENTIAL to national UNITY, communal harmony, and JUSTICE. So the secular character was shaped by Partition, communal conflict, and India's religious diversity. So option 1 is correct.

stem: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar famously described one particular provision as the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution. This was the __________.
options: Right to Constitutional Remedies (the right to move the courts to enforce fundamental rights, e.g., through writs)
Directive Principles
Preamble
Language provision
solution: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar famously described the RIGHT to CONSTITUTIONAL REMEDIES (the fundamental right that allows a citizen to move the courts — including the Supreme Court, through writs — to ENFORCE the other fundamental rights) as the 'HEART and SOUL of the Constitution'. He regarded it as the most important right, because without an effective remedy to enforce them, the other fundamental rights would be meaningless. So the 'heart and soul' provision is the Right to Constitutional Remedies. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The overall achievement of the Constituent Assembly, despite operating amid crisis, is best described as __________.
options: Crafting a durable, democratic Constitution that has provided the framework for the world's largest democracy and adapted to changing needs while preserving its core ideals
Producing a document that was immediately discarded
Failing to complete any constitution
Creating a temporary set of rules for one year only
solution: The overall ACHIEVEMENT of the Constituent Assembly — accomplished despite operating amid the CRISIS of Partition, communal violence, and immense poverty and diversity — is best described as the crafting of a DURABLE, DEMOCRATIC Constitution. This Constitution has provided the enduring FRAMEWORK for the world's LARGEST DEMOCRACY, has proven capable of ADAPTING to changing needs (through amendments and interpretation) over the decades, while PRESERVING its CORE IDEALS (democracy, justice, liberty, equality, fraternity, secularism, and the rule of law). Its longevity and resilience are a testament to the framers' wisdom and foresight. So the Assembly's achievement was a durable, democratic Constitution for the world's largest democracy. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The words 'Socialist' and 'Secular' were added to the Preamble of the Constitution __________.
options: Later, by the 42nd Amendment in 1976 (they were not in the original 1950 Preamble)
In the original Preamble of 1950
By the British before 1947
Never — they are not in the Constitution
solution: The words 'SOCIALIST' and 'SECULAR' were NOT part of the ORIGINAL Preamble adopted in 1949–50 (which described India as a 'Sovereign Democratic Republic'). They were ADDED LATER, by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment in 1976 (during the Emergency), so that the Preamble now describes India as a 'Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic'. (India's secular character, however, was regarded as implicit in the Constitution from the beginning.) So these words were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). This is a prelims-relevant point.

stem: The Constituent Assembly also served, until the first general elections, as __________.
options: The provisional Parliament (the interim legislature) of independent India
The Supreme Court
A princely council
A committee of the British Parliament
solution: Besides framing the Constitution, the Constituent Assembly also functioned as the PROVISIONAL PARLIAMENT (interim legislature) of independent India — making laws and conducting the ordinary legislative business of the new nation — until the first general elections were held (1951–52) and a regular elected Parliament came into being. It thus wore two hats: constitution-maker and interim legislature. So the Assembly also served as the provisional Parliament. This is a prelims-relevant fact.

stem: The vision of the Constitution, drawing on the freedom struggle, was ultimately to __________.
options: Build a democratic, just, and inclusive nation in which all citizens would be free and equal, and the poor and oppressed would be uplifted
Restore colonial rule
Concentrate all wealth in a few hands
Divide citizens permanently by birth
solution: The overarching VISION of the Constitution — drawing directly on the ideals of the FREEDOM STRUGGLE and the aspirations expressed in the Objectives Resolution and Preamble — was to BUILD a DEMOCRATIC, JUST, and INCLUSIVE nation: a republic in which ALL citizens would be FREE and EQUAL (enjoying liberty, equality, and fraternity), the DIGNITY of the individual would be assured, and the POOR and OPPRESSED (including the depressed classes, tribes, women, and minorities) would be UPLIFTED and given justice and opportunity. It aimed to transform India into a society founded on freedom, equality, and social justice. So the vision was to build a democratic, just, inclusive nation uplifting the poor and oppressed. So option 1 is correct.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Framing the Constitution: The Beginning of a New Era' is that:
options: The Indian Constitution was imposed by the British without any Indian involvement

The Indian Constitution was framed between 1946 and 1949 by a Constituent Assembly of Indians (with figures like Dr. Rajendra Prasad as President, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar chairing the Drafting Committee, and Nehru moving the Objectives Resolution) working through committees, expert advice, and prolonged debate; amid the trauma of Partition, its members reconciled deep differences over issues like federalism (opting for a strong Centre), language (the Hindi–English compromise), and the rights and safeguards of minorities and the depressed classes (abolishing untouchability, providing reservations), through consensus and compromise, producing a democratic, secular, inclusive Constitution embodying the ideals of justice, liberty, equality, and fraternity — a foundational document (best studied through the Constituent Assembly Debates) that inaugurated a new era for independent India
The Constitution had no ideals and was written carelessly
The Constitution established a monarchy
solution: The chapter's overall message is that the Indian Constitution was framed by Indians themselves, through a remarkable process of deliberation, between 1946 and 1949 (adopted 26 November 1949; in force 26 January 1950). The CONSTITUENT ASSEMBLY — with Dr. Rajendra PRASAD as its President, Dr. B.R. AMBEDKAR as Chairman of the Drafting Committee (the chief architect), and Jawaharlal NEHRU moving the visionary OBJECTIVES RESOLUTION — accomplished its task through numerous COMMITTEES, expert advice (e.g., B.N. Rau), and PROLONGED, careful DEBATE (preserved in the invaluable Constituent Assembly Debates). Working amid the TRAUMA of PARTITION and communal violence, the members grappled with and RECONCILED deep DIFFERENCES over crucial issues — FEDERALISM (favouring a strong Centre to preserve national unity), LANGUAGE (the Hindi–English compromise, with recognition of regional languages), and the RIGHTS and SAFEGUARDS of minorities and the depressed classes (abolishing untouchability, providing reservations/reserved seats, and adopting secularism) — through a spirit of CONSENSUS and COMPROMISE in the larger national interest. The outcome was a DEMOCRATIC, SECULAR, and INCLUSIVE Constitution embodying the ideals of JUSTICE, LIBERTY, EQUALITY, and FRATERNITY, and guaranteeing fundamental rights. This foundational document — best studied through the Constituent Assembly Debates — marked the BEGINNING of a NEW ERA for independent, republican India. So the overall message is option 2.
